dataset.name: NGEE Arctic Soil Micro-warming Experiment Temperature Profiles, Council Road Mile Marker 71, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2017-2019
description: The reported soil temperature profile measurements (24 locations - 2 probes with 5 and 6 thermistors, respectively - Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) were initiated as part of a soil micro-warming experiment at the Council Road Mile Marker 71 Site (CN_MM71) in September 2017. From 2017 through August 2019, these were measurements of ambient pre-treatment plot conditions. This tussock tundra site (with underlying permafrost) experiences annual frost heaving that causes a vertical movement of the ground surface, hence causing some of the upper most temperature thermistors to be at surface level or above ground and recorded therefore air temperatures near the surface and not below ground soil temperature (see section on Quality Assurance). After August 2019, these measurements ended in preparation for transitioning to the experimental warming of individual plots. The reported temperature data are nominally 3-hour averages of measurements made at varying frequencies (3-hour maximum) with frequencies that depended upon power (solar) availability to operate the sensors (see section in documentation on Methods). The number of values and the standard deviation for each 3-hour average (where appropriate) are also provided. These measurements are located near the NGEE-Arctic CO2 and CH4 eddy covariance tower at the Council Road Site (US-NGC: NGEE Arctic Council, https://ameriflux.lbl.gov/sites/siteinfo/US-NGC#overview) and auxiliary data at https://doi.org/10.5440/1526749. This dataset contains four *.csv files and one *.pdf file.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research. The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

measurementTechnique: Experimental DesignThere are 24 measurement locations (plots) distributed evenly between the dry-ish upland tussock tundra area and wet, flooded water channels (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). Each plot is equipped with two multi-sensor temperature probes (10 cm apart) -- one from 0 to 0.7 m depth with 5 thermistors (measuring at 10, 20, 35, 50 and 70 cm depth) and a second from 0 to 1.0 m with 6 thermistors (measuring at 10, 20, 35, 50, 70 and 100 cm depth), reporting from 11 points total (Fig. 2). These depth distributions were chosen in preparation for a micro warming experiment where one probe will be 10 cm and the second probe 20 cm away from the soil heating rod. MeasurementsTemperature probes were all installed early September 2017 powered by small solar panels, and data logged onto Campbell Scientific CR1000 dataloggers. Power was applied to the probes only when measurements were taken. This means during periods when snow was coving the solar panels and batteries were drained no data was collected. Power and data flow were daisy-chained, meaning that when power was exhausted in the middle of a round of measurements the remaining measurements in the chain were not completed. This also applies when the data or power cable were severed by rodent activity. A malfunctioning probe did not impact data or power flow to/from the remaining probes in the line. During the fall freeze-up and spring thaw periods (the site is only accessible 4 month a year) the measurement interval was set to 3 hours to conserve power while ensuring that at least one round (all 24 locations) of measurements was collected.Quality AssuranceOutlier RemovalAll data (Fig. 3) were quality controlled by removing outliers from malfunctioning thermistors and readings that were beyond realistic temperature limits prior to being averaged (where applicable/possible, see Fig. 4) to export 3-hourly soil temperature data.Frost HeavingThe site experiences annual frost heaving that causes a vertical movement of the ground surface causing buried instrumentation to be pushed up with some of the upper most temperature thermistors to be above ground and record air temperatures near the surface and not below ground soil temperatures (Fig. 5 and Fig. 6). Impacted by this upward movement were probe G in 2018 and probes I, B, K, E, V, O, J, C, S and W in 2019 (Table 2 and Fig 1). These measurements are visualized together with air temperature (Fig. 6) identifying the timing from which individual probes are affected as data have not been filtered for the effect of frost heave. The high discrepancy between air temperature measured at the NGEE-Arctic meteorological station at the site and those reported by these thermistors are caused due to the lack of radiation shielding (insolation effect) of the soil temperature probes.Transition to Micro-Warming ExperimentThe temperature measurement system (not the probes) are reconfigured for a micro-warming experiment in 2019/2020 where two adjacent plots (see Fig. 1) are paired into blocks with each having a control and a treatment (heated) plot. At a treatment plot, one probe will be 10 cm and the second probe 20 cm away from the soil heating rod. The new configuration will also include soil moisture and CO2 soil flux using forced diffusion chamber technique measurements at each plot and part of a new/different data package.
